subjects.displayTitle: The soul’s immortality: arguments, images, and the limits of sight
subjects.introduction: A broken cage need not mean the death of its bird: this image opens an inquiry into the relation between the body and the soul. The readings develop arguments from composition, thought, identity, dreams, and enduring spiritual influence. They also distinguish fruitful insight from delusion and acknowledge the place of faith in approaching a world beyond present experience. Their reasoning asks readers to examine premises as well as conclusions, attending to the different work done by an analogy, an observation, and a theological claim. Plato’s Phaedo offers a comparison through its argument about the soul’s affinity with what is unseen and unchanging [1]. Connected subjects explore rational arguments, the soul’s existence, and life after death. Together they invite a patient investigation of what these arguments establish, what they presuppose, and how reflection on immortality might shape the way a person lives.
subjects.arc: Begin with the bird and cage and the invitation to reason, distinguish soul from bodily instruments, examine composition and enduring effects, then explore dreams, discernment, faith, and wider philosophical voices.

subjects.displayTitle: Contentment: a tranquil heart and an active life
subjects.introduction: Can the heart find rest while the hands remain busy? These readings place contentment alongside effort, practical care, gratitude, and service. They acknowledge the difficulty of acquiescence, the persistence of human feeling, and the sorrow of separation. Their prayers approach uncertainty through a relationship with God, whose purposes exceed the present wishes of the petitioner. Repeated images of sweetness in bitterness invite reflection on the transformation of experience through love; they also require attentive reading in their particular settings. Epictetus offers a comparison through his distinction between what is within our control and what lies beyond it [1]. Connected subjects—composure, detachment, humility, piety, tests, and gratitude—help unfold different dimensions of this discipline. Read together, these passages ask how trust can sustain responsible action, and how a person might cultivate peace while remaining tender toward suffering.
subjects.arc: Open with effort and practical care, acknowledge emotional difficulty and grief, explore freedom from attachment and limits of foresight, then follow gratitude, endurance, and prayer toward loving trust.

subjects.displayTitle: Consultation: thinking together and acting in unity
subjects.introduction: An idea can become more useful when its speaker is willing to release it. These readings approach consultation as a shared search for truth, sustained by humility, careful listening, freedom of expression, and love. They bring discussion into practical affairs: education, livelihood, family decisions, community meetings, and organized service. Alongside the invitation to speak candidly come responsibilities for deliberation, wise discretion, collective decisions, and learning through experience. Particular historical arrangements remain part of the record and invite attention to their setting. The Qur’an places mutual counsel alongside prayer and generosity [1], offering a related religious perspective on communal life. Connected subjects explore diversity and unity of thought, fellowship, spiritual assemblies, and gatherings. Together they invite readers to ask how disagreement can yield understanding, and how commitment to a common decision can coexist with openness to correction.
subjects.arc: Begin with releasing attachment to an opinion, establish truth-seeking and spiritual qualities, consider disagreement and decision, then follow consultation into institutions, practical responsibilities, and shared learning.
